findings.title: The EPFO ECR declares EPF wages of basic+DA while the contribution remitted was computed on the higher s.2(y) wage base — the file cannot reconcile
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_compute_slip (line ~968) computes the PF base as `_wb = wage_base.compute(...)` then `pf_wages = _wb.wages_paise + ot.pf_wages_paise`, and stores `pf_wages_paise` on the slip. domain/payroll/ecr.py::build_ecr (line ~239) IGNORES that stored column and re-derives `pf_wages = basic_paise + da_paise + one_time_pf_wages_paise`. I ran it: employee on basic 10,000 + HRA 18,000, FY 2026-27 month 6 → slip pf_wages_paise=1400000 (14,000, addback 4,000), pf_employee 1,680, employer EPS 1,166 / EPF 514; build_ecr emits EPF_WAGES=10000 with EPF_CONTRI=2194 and EPS=1166 — an implied contribution rate of 33.6% of the wages declared. The module's own comment two lines above warns "Omitting it here would file EPF wages lower than the 12% remitted against them, which the portal reconciles and rejects." No test in tests/test_epfo_ecr.py or tests/test_the_pf_wage_base_under_the_labour_codes.py asserts wages-vs-contribution consistency.
findings.ca_experience: Every employee whose basic+DA is below the ₹15,000 ceiling on a low-basic/high-HRA structure — the ordinary Indian structure at those salary levels — gets an ECR line the EPFO portal rejects, or accepts as a false wage declaration. The CA discovers it on the 15th, at the portal, after the run is finalised and the journal posted. The GL, the payslip and the challan say one number; the return says another.
findings.market_standard: greytHR, Keka and Zoho Payroll generate the ECR from the same wage figure the contribution was computed on; the EPFO portal reconciles wages against contributions on upload and rejects the batch on a mismatch.
findings.suggested_fix: In build_ecr, read `slip['pf_wages_paise'] + slip['one_time_pf_wages_paise']` (falling back to basic+da for pre-migration-334 slips where pf_wages_rule_applied is false/absent) instead of re-deriving. Add a test that asserts epf_contribution ≈ 12% of epf_wages for every member in the file.

findings.title: A draft payroll run that was never finalised is counted as TDS already deducted, months already paid and gross already paid in the next month's §192 projection
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_tds_already_deducted_this_fy (lines 700-753) reads `db.table("payroll_runs").select("id, month").eq(firm).eq(client)` with NO status filter, then sums `tds_paise`, counts months and sums `gross_paise` from those runs' slips. `_members_contributing_earlier_this_period` (lines 442-446) does the same for ESI Rule 50 coverage. By contrast _assemble_24q_source:4142 and form_24q_annexure_ii:4353 both filter `status in ("finalized","paid")`, and migration 323 draws the same line for RLS. There is no DELETE /runs/{id} and no recompute endpoint anywhere in routers/payroll.py, so an abandoned draft sits in the table permanently.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who creates a draft run for September to look at the numbers and then abandons it (there is no way to delete it) makes October, November and every later month under-withhold: `_months_remaining_for_spread` shortens, and the September draft's TDS is credited as if deposited. §192(1) makes the EMPLOYER liable for the shortfall and §201(1A) charges 1% a month on it. Nothing on the payslip looks wrong. Meanwhile the 24Q built from the same data excludes September, so the return and the withholding disagree.
findings.market_standard: greytHR and Zoho Payroll compute YTD tax credits from PROCESSED/approved payroll only; an unapproved run contributes nothing.
findings.suggested_fix: Add `.in_("status", _PAYROLL_RELEASED)` to both reads, matching the 24Q/Annexure II/ECR/RLS line. Separately, add a way to discard or recompute a draft run.

verification.what_is_actually_true: Both reads genuinely lack the `status in ('finalized','paid')` filter that 24Q (routers/payroll.py:4142, :4345) and migration 323 apply, so a draft month is treated as paid by the s.192 projection and by ESI Rule 50 coverage, and the return and the withholding then disagree about which months exist. But the consequence is the opposite of the one claimed: measured through create_run on the FakeDB harness, an abandoned September draft leaves the year OVER-withheld by Rs 38,350 (Rs 6,07,750 taken against Rs 5,69,400 due on 11 months), and October's figure is unchanged to the paise. The genuine defects are the inconsistency itself and the absence of any way to discard or recompute a draft run.
verification.probe: python -m pytest scratchpad/probe_pay04b.py -s -> 'WITH abandoned Sept draft -> October TDS: 5525000' / 'WITHOUT the Sept draft -> October TDS: 5525000' (identical). probe_pay04c.py -> 'sum EXCLUDING abandoned Sep: 607750.0' vs 'true annual tax on 11 months = 33L: 569400.0'. probe_pay04.py -> 'YTD as seen by October (draft September still counted): {e-1: (0, 1, 10000000)}' with run status 'draft'.

lens_notes.literal: The code claim is exact. routers/payroll.py:715-717 (_tds_already_deducted_this_fy) and :442-444 (_members_contributing_earlier_this_period) both do `db.table("payroll_runs").select("id, month").eq(firm).eq(client)` with no status predicate, then sum tds_paise/gross_paise and count months off those runs' slips. The contrast is real: _assemble_24q_source filters `r.get("status") in ("finalized","paid")` at :4142, form_24q_annexure_ii at :4345, and migration 323 line 56 has `AND r.status IN ('finalized','paid')`. There is no DELETE /runs/{id} and no recompute endpoint — the full @router listing for routers/payroll.py contains no run delete, and create_run:1744 rejects a second run for the same (firm, client, month) with 409, so an abandoned draft is permanent. THE HARM CLAIM IS WRONG IN DIRECTION, though. I ran the real create_run against the FakeDB harness: October's TDS is IDENTICAL (Rs 55,250) with and without an abandoned September draft, because the shortened `_months_remaining_for_spread` and the credited draft TDS cancel exactly. Over a whole year with September abandoned, the employee actually has Rs 6,07,750 withheld across the 11 months paid, against a true tax of Rs 5,69,400 on 11 months of salary — Rs 38,350 OVER-withheld, not under. So there is no s.192(1) shortfall and no s.201(1A) interest; the phantom month's gross inflates the projection by more than the phantom month's TDS credit reduces it.
lens_notes.guards: create_run's UNIQUE (firm, client, month) index (migration 237, translated to a 409 at :1744-1764) bounds the blast radius to at most one stale run per month. _tds_already_deducted_this_fy's own docstring notes the failure mode is deliberately biased to over-deduct. Nothing filters status, and no test covers a draft-vs-finalised distinction on either read.
lens_notes.reach: Reached — create_run is the only way to make a run and both helpers are called from it (:1808, :1817-1818). But the scenario needs an abandoned run, and because the only way to pay September is to finalise the very draft in question, a permanently abandoned draft is an unusual rather than routine state.

As the 7 September verification established, the harm is the inconsistency plus the absence of any way to discard or recompute a draft (see PAY-21), not the over-withholding the original finding claimed.

findings.title: pt_applicable with no pt_state withholds zero professional tax and is reported as a gap by nothing — and the client-workspace form creates employees in exactly that state
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_compute_pt returns 0 for an unrecognised/empty state. _statutory_gaps (line 356) only appends when `classify_pt_state(...).is_gap`; I ran domain/payroll/professional_tax.classify_state(None) → `is_gap False, note 'No state set; no professional tax withheld.'`. domain/payroll/exceptions.py:123-130 uses the same classify_state, so the exception index misses it too. apps/web/app/clients/[id]/payroll/page.tsx:457-462 renders a `pt_applicable` checkbox and NEVER collects pt_state (the field does not appear in that form at all), and addEmployee (line 358) posts the payload straight through.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who adds an employee from the client workspace and ticks "PT" gets ₹0 professional tax withheld every month, forever, with no gap on the run, no line on the exception index, and nothing on the payslip. Article 276 makes the employer liable for the shortfall with interest. This is precisely the "a zero for Delhi and a zero for Gujarat are the same number meaning opposite things" failure the whole gap mechanism was built to prevent, reintroduced through the one form that does not collect the state.
findings.market_standard: greytHR and Zoho Payroll make the PT work-location mandatory before PT can be enabled on an employee.
findings.suggested_fix: Two changes: (a) classify_state must report `is_gap=True` when pt_applicable is set and the state is blank — the caller already knows pt_applicable; (b) add pt_state to the client-workspace employee form and refuse pt_applicable without it in EmployeeIn.

verification.what_is_actually_true: pt_applicable with a blank pt_state withholds zero and produces no gap and no exception, because classify_state treats 'no state' as a correct zero (domain/payroll/professional_tax.py:96-99) without knowing pt_applicable was set, and the client-workspace add-employee form (apps/web/app/clients/[id]/payroll/page.tsx:270, :459-465) is the one path that can create exactly that row. Severity is medium rather than high because the other creation path (components/payroll/AddEmployeeModal.tsx:109-110) makes pt_applicable derivative of a mandatory state and cannot produce it, and Article 276(2) caps the exposure at Rs 2,500 per employee per year.

findings.title: The §10(13A) HRA salary base is annualised as this month × 12 regardless of how many months the employee actually works — a mid-year joiner's exemption computes to zero
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_compute_slip line ~1050 passes `basic_plus_da_paise=(basic + da) * 12` and `hra_received_paise=hra * 12` to _monthly_tds, while the income figure two lines above correctly uses `recurring * months_left + gross_already_paid_paise`. I ran it: an old-regime employee joining 1 Oct 2026 on basic ₹1,00,000 + 50% HRA, rent ₹1,20,000 for the six months — HRADetails with the 12-month base returns an exemption of ₹0 (rent 1.2L minus 10% of a fabricated 12L salary), with the correct 6-month base it returns ₹60,000.
findings.ca_experience: Every mid-year joiner on the old regime who claims HRA loses their entire §10(13A) exemption in the withholding, because the "rent paid less 10% of salary" limb is computed against twice the salary they will earn. On the worked figures that is ~₹18,700 over-withheld across six months, recoverable only on assessment a year later — the same class of error, and the same direction, as the twelve-month projection bug the 1 September audit fixed. The mid-year raise case is wrong the same way.
findings.market_standard: greytHR, Keka and Zoho Payroll compute the §10(13A) limbs on the salary and HRA for the period the rent relates to, per Rule 2A.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `(basic + da) * months_employed_in_fy` and `hra * months_employed_in_fy`, or better, accumulate actual paid basic/DA/HRA from the year's slips plus the projected remainder — the same shape annual_gross already uses.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The s.10(13A) salary and HRA bases are annualised as this month x 12 (routers/payroll.py:1046-1047) while the projected income the same call uses is months-employed aware (:1014, :1033-1035). For an employee joining 1 Oct 2026 on Rs 1,00,000 basic with 50% HRA and Rs 1,20,000 rent, the x12 base zeroes the exemption entirely; the correct 6-month base gives Rs 60,000. findings.title: Reversing a payroll run does not restore employee loan balances, so re-finalising the same run recovers the instalment twice
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:finalize_run:2314 calls `_apply_loan_recoveries(db, firm_id, client_id, run_id)` after the journal posts; that function (line 568) reduces `payroll_loans.outstanding_paise` by each slip's `loan_recovery_paise` and closes the loan at zero. reverse_run (line 2431) reverses both journals and resets status/journal ids — it never touches payroll_loans and never mentions them. The slips are not deleted, so a second finalize_run re-reads the same `loan_recovery_paise` and applies it again. The docstring of _apply_loan_recoveries explicitly reasons that finalisation "is guarded against running twice" — reverse_run removes that guard.
findings.ca_experience: A CA who reverses August to correct something and re-finalises has written the employee's advance down twice. The loan closes early, the employee is shown a nil balance they still owe, and the ledger's Employee Loans receivable is understated by the instalment. Nothing on any screen says it happened.
findings.market_standard: Zoho Payroll and greytHR reverse loan/advance amortisation entries when a payroll run is rolled back.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the inverse write to reverse_run (add the recovered amount back and clear closed_on), or make the write-down idempotent by recording the run_id against each loan repayment rather than mutating a running balance.

findings.title: A leaver's settlement TDS never reaches the quarterly 24Q, though it does reach the annual Annexure II — so Annexure I and Annexure II disagree
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_assemble_24q_source (lines 4136-4165) builds slips_by_month purely from `payroll_runs` → `payroll_slips`; `payroll_settlements` is never queried. form_24q_annexure_ii:4380-4400 DOES read payroll_settlements and adds `settled['tds_paise']` to the annual TDS. record_settlement:5330 computes and stores a §192 withholding on the settlement (`tds` column) and posts it to TDS Payable - Salary via journal_for_settlement. docs/audits/2026-09-01-payroll-can-it-run-a-year.md claims "its TDS reaches 24Q".
findings.ca_experience: A CA who settles a leaver in, say, November deposits the TDS on the challan but files Q3's 24Q short by that amount. The challan will not reconcile against the deductee rows, and the employee gets no 26AS credit for the deduction until the Q4 Annexure II — which will then show a TDS total larger than the sum of the four quarters' Annexure I. TRACES flags this as a short-deduction default.
findings.market_standard: Winman TDS, ClearTax and Saral build Annexure I from every deduction in the quarter, terminal payments included.
findings.suggested_fix: In _assemble_24q_source, read payroll_settlements for the quarter's months and emit a deductee row per settlement (payment_date = leaving/payment date, amount = taxable_paise, tds = tds_paise), joined to the same PAN checks.

findings.title: Annual professional tax for §16(iii) is estimated as this month's PT × 12 — six times the year's real liability in a Tamil Nadu September, zero in every other month
findings.evidence: routers/payroll.py:_compute_slip line ~1053 passes `professional_tax_paise=pt * 12`. _compute_pt_tn (line 283) returns the whole half-yearly amount in months 9 and 3 and zero otherwise; _compute_pt_mh returns ₹300 in February and ₹200 otherwise. I ran an old-regime TN employee on ₹50,000 basic: month 8 pt=0 tds=₹6,110; month 9 pt=₹1,250 tds=₹5,850; month 10 pt=0 tds=₹6,110 — September claims ₹15,000 of §16(iii) against a real annual PT of ₹2,500.
findings.ca_experience: An old-regime employee in Tamil Nadu has their TDS drop by ~₹260 in September and March and revert in between, because the deduction claimed is 6× the year's actual PT. findings.title: §80CCD(2)'s 14%/10% cap is applied to gross salary instead of basic+DA, so a large employer-NPS declaration can be over-allowed

findings.ca_experience: An employee who declares an employer NPS contribution under §80CCD(2) is allowed up to 14% of GROSS rather than 14% of basic+DA. On a 40%-basic structure that is more than double the statutory cap, and it under-withholds — a §192(1) shortfall the employer answers for. It binds only where the declared NPS figure is large, so it will not show up on most employees.
findings.market_standard: greytHR and Zoho compute the §80CCD(2) cap on basic+DA per the Explanation to §80CCD.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass `salary_for_80ccd2_paise=(basic + da) * months_employed_in_fy` from _compute_slip through _monthly_tds into the declaration request.

findings.title: The payroll journal posts one Salaries Expense account and defines the debit as the sum of the credits
findings.evidence: services/phase2_journal_service.py:_build_payroll_lines:813-890 — a single `%Salaries Expense%` debit whose amount is the sum of net + PF (incl. EDLI and admin) + ESI + PT + TDS + loans, with the docstring conceding "Employer PF/ESI is folded into Salaries Expense here… A future enhancement could split it into a dedicated 'Contribution to PF & Other Funds' account for the Schedule III employee-benefit sub-classification". docs/audits/2026-09-01 itself warns that "defining the debit as the sum of the credits is exactly how the payroll accrual's own missing-credit-leg bug stayed hidden" — and the accrual still does it.
findings.ca_experience: Schedule III requires Employee benefits expense split into (a) salaries and wages, (b) contribution to provident and other funds, (c) staff welfare. This product produces a trial balance that cannot be mapped to that note without manual analysis, in a platform whose whole pitch is that payroll posts into the ledger the CA already closes. And a missing credit leg is undetectable by construction, because the debit is derived from the credits.
findings.market_standard: Tally Prime and Zoho Books post salaries, employer PF, employer ESI and staff welfare to separate ledgers so Schedule III maps directly.
findings.suggested_fix: Split into Salaries and Wages / Contribution to PF and Other Funds (employer PF + EPS + EDLI + admin) / Contribution to ESI, compute the debit independently from the slip components, and let the kernel's balance assertion catch a disagreement.

verification.what_is_actually_true: The payroll accrual posts employer PF, EPS, EDLI, the admin charge and employer ESI inside a single Salaries Expense debit defined as the sum of the credits (services/phase2_journal_service.py:888,908-910), and no report re-splits them, so the Schedule III employee-benefits sub-classification needs manual analysis. The finding's 'undetectable by construction' limb is refuted: services/phase2_journal_service.py:900-906 carries an explicit range invariant that fails a run whose credits do not add up, though its tolerance is the employer-contribution band rather than an exact identity.
verification.probe: Read of services/phase2_journal_service.py:813-915 (single salary_exp debit; the ValueError guard at 902-906) and domain/reporting/schedule_iii.py:344-372 (one 'Employee Benefit Expense' line, no sub-note). grep -rn 'Contribution to PF' across apps/api → only the docstring at phase2_journal_service.py:827.

lens_notes.literal: The main claim is exact: services/phase2_journal_service.py:813-915 builds ONE debit to '%Salaries Expense%' whose amount is `total_cost = sum(amount for _, amount, _ in credits)` (line 888) — net + PF (with EDLI and the admin charge) + ESI + PT + TDS + loan recovery — and the docstring at :826-829 concedes the Schedule III split is 'a future enhancement'. There is no employee-benefits sub-classification anywhere downstream either: domain/reporting/schedule_iii.py:349,367 emits a single 'Employee Benefit Expense' line with no note breaking it into salaries and wages / contribution to provident and other funds / staff welfare.
lens_notes.guards: One limb of the finding is WRONG. 'A missing credit leg is undetectable by construction' is refuted by services/phase2_journal_service.py:900-906, an explicit invariant that raises ValueError('Payroll journal identity violated ... a deduction is missing a credit leg') unless gross <= total_cost <= gross + pf + esi + edli + pf_admin. It is a band rather than an equality, so a missing credit leg smaller than the employer's own contributions would still pass — but the case the finding says is undetectable is in fact detected for anything larger than that. Staff welfare is also already a separate ledger in the seeded chart (services/coa_seed_service.py:108, account 5013 'Staff Welfare'), so the conflation is confined to employer PF/EPS/EDLI/admin and employer ESI being inside Salaries Expense.
lens_notes.reach: Every finalised run posts through this path (journal_for_payroll, services/phase2_journal_service.py:837+), and the resulting trial balance feeds domain/reporting/schedule_iii.py, so it reaches the year-end statements a CA files.

maturity.rationale: This is the sharpest split in the codebase: a genuinely excellent statutory engine behind a surface that cannot reach half of it, plus a small number of wrong numbers that reach a CA. The engine deserves a B+/A- on its own — twenty-six domain modules, 743 passing payroll tests, §192 as a real projection with §192(3) adjustment, the three §115BAC objects kept apart, ESI Rule 50 contribution periods, the Code on Wages s.2(y) PF base with a period test, gratuity §4(2) at the day boundary, a named-gap discipline that refuses rather than guesses, and a release that blocks on unresolved gaps with a typed Partner override on a transition log. Almost nothing in the Indian market reasons this carefully. But the grade is what a CA would experience, and a CA would experience: an ECR whose wage column cannot reconcile with the contribution remitted (PAY-01), an Annexure II that gives old-regime employees the wrong §16(ia) and so produces a wrong Form 16 Part B (PAY-02), payslips headed with the accountant's name instead of the employer's (PAY-03), no way to settle a leaver or produce the year-end annexure from any screen (PAY-11), and no way to enter LOP from the client's own payroll tab (PAY-15). The owner's instinct about the client-workspace tab is correct and the evidence is specific: it has five well-designed verbs and the Inputs verb has no inputs in it. The docs are ahead of the code in two places that matter — the 1 September audit says the leaver is "wired" (the endpoint is; no screen calls it) and that the module can run a year (it cannot produce the year-end Annexure II from any screen).
maturity.would_a_ca_buy_this_module_alone: Not yet — a CA could not run a full year on it today, because the leaver settlement, the salary revision, the employee advance and the Annexure II that becomes Form 16 exist only as endpoints with no screen, and the ECR they would upload on the 15th declares a wage the contribution does not reconcile to.

open_questions_for_owner: The 1 April 2027 cutover in docs/architecture/10-payroll.md rests on there being no mid-year opening-position import. Is that still the plan? If yes, PAY-04 (draft runs credited as TDS deducted) and PAY-21 (no way to recompute or discard a run) become urgent, because they are the two ways the first real month can go wrong with nothing on screen saying so. If the plan has moved to a mid-year start, `payroll_opening_positions` does not exist in any migration and the §192 projection withholds from a fiction.

Seven finished capabilities have no screen (PAY-11). Which order do you want them in? My reading of the calendar is Annexure II first (it is the year-end deliverable and June 2028 is the first hard date), then settlement, then salary revisions — but if the beachhead cohort has high churn, settlement is first.

The design doc says payroll becomes the 13th top-level workspace with a Setup screen that publishes PT/LWF state coverage. Neither exists, and the firm-recorded-PT-slabs endpoints (PUT /statutory-values/pt) have no caller. Is the state-coverage screen still the intended answer to the bundling problem, or has that been reconsidered?

The payslip currently carries the CA firm's name (PAY-03). Fixing it means deciding what a bureau payslip should say: employer only, or employer with a small 'processed by <firm>' line? That is a commercial decision, not a technical one.

Leave is half-built and the invented 12/12/15 defaults reach the employee portal (PAY-24). The design doc defers leave management. Do you want it removed until there is a policy model, or is a minimal per-client leave policy in scope?

Statutory bonus is computed only for leavers (PAY-23). Bonus is an annual obligation for every eligible employee under §19 of the Bonus Act. Is an annual bonus run in scope for the first cohort, or is the expectation that the CA does it outside the product for year one?

Two payroll deadline calendars exist, one in the backend compliance engine and one written in TypeScript on two payroll pages (PAY-19). The frontend one invents a professional-tax due date that compliance_engine deliberately refuses and that a test pins as absent. Do you want the payroll pages to render the engine's dates, or should payroll have no calendar of its own and point at /deadlines?

What is the realistic size of the first cohort — clients per firm, employees per client, months of history? PAY-16 (every slip of every run loaded into the browser) is harmless at seven clients and fatal at forty, and knowing the number decides whether that is a now-fix or a later-fix.

Is there an appetite for a small parity-test discipline between what the run computes and what each statutory file declares? PAY-01 and PAY-20 are both one implementation drifting from another, and the codebase already has the pattern (tests/test_cash_flow_sql_parity_pg.py, tests/test_schedule_iii_ageing_parity_pg.py) — it just was not applied to the ECR.
strengths: The §192 engine is genuinely ahead of the Indian market. routers/payroll.py:_months_employed_in_fy + _compute_slip project the year as what has actually been paid plus this month's rate times the months still to come, and _months_remaining_for_spread applies §192(3) against what THIS deductor has already withheld, degrading to annual/12 when there is no history — the docstring at line 1113 works through why counting from the calendar instead would double every payslip's TDS for a mid-year onboarding.

The three §115BAC objects are kept genuinely separate and nothing sets one from another. domain/payroll/declarations.py:1-70 distinguishes the Circular 04/2023 intimation (withholding), the §115BAC(6) election (the return, in domain/income_tax/regime_election.py) and the Rule 26C Form 12BB evidence, and `notices()` tells the CA that an old-regime intimation is not the election. Almost every payroll product conflates the first two.

The declared-versus-verified split is real and correctly gated. domain/payroll/declarations.py:DeclarationItem.effective_paise plus routers/payroll.py:PROOF_CUTOFF_MONTH_OF_FY=10 and _verified_only_from_month stop an unproved claim reducing tax from January, which is exactly where §192(1) liability bites; migration 297 enforces the same line in RLS so an employee filing through the portal cannot set a *_verified_paise column or proofs_verified.

The named-gap discipline is the module's best idea and it is applied consistently. _statutory_gaps, _attendance_gap, _age_gap and identity_domain.pt_registration_gaps all distinguish 'nothing is due' from 'something is due and nobody worked it out', and migration 328 turned that from advice into a block: finalize_run RECOMPUTES the gaps (routers/payroll.py:_release_gaps) so a CA who has since closed one is not still refused, and an override needs a 20-character typed reason on payroll_run_transitions.

The PF wage base under the Labour Codes is modelled properly and period-aware. domain/payroll/wage_base.py implements the Code on Wages s.2(y) proviso as a cap on exclusions with a deemed add-back, classifies only HRA (clause f) and LTA (clause d) as excluded with the reasoning for defaulting everything else to wages (citing RPFC v. Vivekananda Vidyamandir), reproduces the old basic+DA exactly for any month ending before 21-11-2025, and is pinned by 16 tests.

The EPS/EPF/EDLI/admin split is stored on the slip rather than recomputed, and the ₹500-per-establishment admin floor is applied on the run total rather than per payslip (domain/payroll/statutory.py:admin_charge_for_establishment, called from both create_run and statutory_position — moved, not copied). Migration 329 got EDLI and the admin charge into the general ledger.

ESI Rule 50 contribution periods are modelled, and the 'was this member covered when the period began' question is answered from payroll history rather than inferred from the current wage (routers/payroll.py:_members_contributing_earlier_this_period + domain/payroll/statutory.py:esi_contribution_period).

Gratuity is careful where it matters: domain/payroll/gratuity.py:completed_service compares by date so 'six months and one day' rounds the year up and six months exactly does not, the daily wage is one division rather than fifteen rounded ones, §4(2)'s 26-day divisor is used, and §10(10)'s lifetime limit is an input with a named gap rather than an assumption.

The statutory files refuse rather than guess, in the right places. domain/payroll/esic.py will not invent a reason code for a zero-wage member; domain/payroll/form24q.py refuses a deductee with no valid PAN because §206AA makes it a short deduction the employer carries; domain/payroll/ecr.py sanitises names against its own #~# delimiter so a name cannot shift the wage columns.

Attendance became a real contract. domain/payroll/attendance.py enforces days_present + paid leave + LOP = working_days and refuses an inconsistent row rather than flooring it, PUT /attendance writes only the employees sent, and migration 324's attendance_entered plus migration 326 mean 'confirmed full month' and 'nobody asked' are no longer the same row.

Tenancy and access are handled seriously on a sensitive surface: _assert_run_scope / _assert_employee_scope / _assert_slip_scope resolve payroll_slips (which has no firm_id) through its run, the firm-wide reads use filter_by_client so an Executive assigned to four clients cannot read forty clients' salaries, and migration 323 stops an employee reading a draft payslip in the RLS policy rather than in a page filter.

Test coverage on the engine is real: 743 payroll-related tests pass in mock mode across 33 test modules, including negative controls (the 1 September audit records mutating the code and requiring a named test to fail), a parity test holding the Python and SQL ageing implementations identical, and frontend guard tests (apps/web/scripts/statutory-files-are-server-built.test.ts) that stop the browser-built ECR coming back.

(2) tests/test_24q_annexure_ii.py passes one STD_DEDUCTION constant and never parametrises the regime, so PAY-02 is green; the test at line 62 asserts the figure passed in, not the figure due. (3) apps/web/scripts/employee-form-captures-what-filing-needs.test.ts asserts joining_date is in the form and passes — while PATCH silently discards it (PAY-12), because the test reads the form file and never the model. (4) statutory-files-are-server-built.test.ts guards app/payroll/page.tsx only; app/payroll/reports/page.tsx still carries the browser-side employer PF/ESI it was written to eliminate (PAY-09). (5) No test covers _tds_already_deducted_this_fy's run-status filter, the loan write-down under reversal, the PT×12 annualisation or the ×12 HRA base. (6) Nothing tests the payslip PDF's employer identity. I found no test asserting a WRONG statutory rule — the tests are honest about what they check; the gap is that they check the domain modules and not the seams between them.
